newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Asia wants monetary cooperation, whatever that means.
newsitem.headline: Asia wants monetary cooperation, whatever that means.

text.p: Financial planners from five Asia-Pacific nations supported greater monetary cooperation at an economic forum in Hong Kong, but exactly what that means and how the idea takes shape remain open to question.
But all agreed that recent bilateral U.S. dollar repurchase agreements between a number of Asian nations do not signal the beginning of an Asian equivalent to monetary union European style.

"Asia is characterised by so much cultural, political, economic and historical diversity that the idea of monetary union is a non-starter," Donald Tsang, Hong Kong's Financial Secretary, said on Wednesday at the 1996 Europe/East Asia summit organised by the World Economic Forum.
But views among the officials from Australia, China, Japan, South Korea and Hong Kong differed on exactly how Asia defines monetary cooperation.

Australia, long a proponent of greater regional cooperation, repeated calls for the creation an Asian equivalent of the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) and added the proposal that domestic Asian banks submit to regional regulation.
"There is a lot of scope for us to get together and agree and make our voices heard," Ian Macfarlane, Governor of the Reserve Bank of Australia, told the forum.
His fellow panellists smiled politely but declined to comment on proposals.
Instead, they concentrated on the ultimate goal of monetary cooperation -- to reduce currency volatility and promote financial and economic stability.
"Monetary co-operation is not an end in itself, but a means to the end of greater prosperity and stability in the region," Tsang said.

Asia has a high savings rate of over 30 percent and huge investment needs, yet a large part of Asian savings have been invested through official reserves in nations belonging to the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development.

"If somehow we could make Asian financial intermediation more efficient, whereby we can apply greater Asian savings to finance Asian investments at lower risks, Asian economies would become far less reliant on fund flows from outside the region and thus far less vulnerable to external shocks," Tsang said.
"Monetary co-operation becomes the key," he said.

If currency stability is the ultimate goal, the United States should be involved because so many Asian nations link their currencies to the U.S. dollar, said Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the Japanese Ministry of Finance's International Finance Bureau.
Asia could also reduce currency risk by dealing with major imbalances in the currency structure of their assets and liabilities, Sakakibara said.
"Instability of the yen and other Asian currencies in the spring of 1995 were at least partially the result of these imbalances," he said.
Tsang insisted that consensus would be required before the future unfolded.
"(The idea) will move forward at a pace comfortable to all," he said. "Consensus is the key and we must all be sensitive to each other's specific concerns."
